how: The poster calls members to fix a blackened logo described as ours, without establishing that anyone joins or places pixels.
After placement ends, a member corrects the post’s attribution of the logo to the room by identifying Northeastern instead.
Coding a call as recruitment for the room’s own work must retain disputed ownership when its reply identifies the target as another group’s logo.
The sole recorded reply corrects ownership rather than joining, assenting, reporting work done, or thanking, establishing no written acceptance within this exchange.
The ownership correction questions attribution rather than the room’s manpower or available space, so its placement supplies no evidence of this condition.
A repair call and an ownership correction cannot establish that members actually worked on a mark without deciding their organization.
Correcting whose logo it is does not establish a dispute about who can bind members to an agreement with another room.
The visible call receives an ownership correction, while acceptance through unreported placing remains unknown and prevents testing the arrow’s full written-or-placing mechanism.
The correction supplies neither a prior interroom agreement nor a dispute about binding members, leaving the tentative transition untested.
A caller seeks repair of an existing logo, but these passages do not identify its starter or establish that others join.
Calling the logo ours supplies a disputed attribution without showing a settled design or an adopted claim to another group’s mark.
The report describes black fill and asks for repair without reporting that members built the mark.
The call names the bottom left corner but provides no pixel coordinates or template, leaving circulation of those tools unobserved.
The call and correction provide no evidence about scripts, bots, or spare accounts.
The poster proposes repairing black fill, but neither concept reports completed repairs or establishes that the room placed or kept this work.
The reply identifies whose logo it is without identifying who changed its pixels or why.
The ownership correction supplies no evidence of border negotiations, truces, or deals.
The correction does not ask members to spare another work, report restraint, or apologise for damage.
Identifying Northeastern as the logo’s owner does not establish help requested, offered, exchanged, or refused between rooms.
The call and correction provide no evidence of a coalition or a joint mark.
The poster reports blackening by unspecified actors without calling for an attack or admitting that room members attacked.
The correction identifies another group without taunts, victory claims, or other evidence of a continuing contest.
The call asks for repair at the existing location without evidence of relocation or a decision to move.
Neither concept celebrates a completed work or credits makers and helpers.
The two concepts describe perceived damage and correct attribution without showing a saved record or a retrospective account of the work’s fate.
Neither concept proposes carrying the effort into a later canvas or another lasting form.
The repair call and ownership correction do not identify either turn as an April Fools joke.
Naming Northeastern as owner does not identify a preexisting rivalry or supply a reason for an attack.
The ownership correction does not carry a prior quarrel into the canvas.
The pronoun ours and its correction do not establish a carried-in ideology, lore, quarrel, or colour allegiance.
The correction attributes the logo to another group without describing guest space or a host’s authority.
The replying member corrects attribution without evidence of carrying a proposal on another room’s behalf.
The two concepts supply no evidence of moderation or members drawing rules around canvas discussion.
